name: Victor Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining, Victor. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the week. I'm on a transmission crew, so the big steel towers carrying high voltage between substations, and we travel all over the region. A typical day is a 5:30 start from a motel, drive to the tower, rig the ropes and swap insulator strings or fix damaged conductor. I love the height and the views, honestly, and the crew's like a travelling family. What wears me out is living out of a bag four nights a week.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, renting a room in a shared house near the bus station. The big cost is the truck loan, a used pickup I needed for the travel days. I've got maybe three weeks of money put by, which is nothing. I use AI every day though, for route planning, reading manuals, even meal plans on the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool like any other. I use it all the time and it's handy, but if it plateaus, it plateaus. I'd post something like that on my crew's group chat and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't really change my problem, which is the truck loan and the company cutting the travel allowance last spring. That cut took about a hundred and fifty a month off me. AI plateauing doesn't fix my truck loan or the travel allowance cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep taking every travel job, and pay the truck loan down faster. I'd try to sell some of the gear I don't use, like the spare climbing kit. And I'd still use the AI tools for planning because they save me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine about AI, a bit tense about money. It's the same tension I've had all year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the travel allowance cut hurt. What did you change after it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Started cooking in the motel microwave instead of eating at the diner. Sounds small, but it's real money over a month. The chatbot helped me plan the meals, funnily enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a job you'd look at if the travel got too much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a local distribution crew, but there aren't many nearby and they pay less. So no, I'd stick it out.

feel: **Fine** about AI but tense about **money**, the same as all year.

fieldNote: He's **comfortable** with AI and uses it daily for small things.

steps.text: Sell the spare climbing kit to pay the truck loan down

Take every travel job on the transmission crew

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where people like us should get ahead. Learn the tools, learn to fly the inspection drones, be the person the company calls. I'd be telling the younger guys to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The paperwork and planning go to software, which I don't care about, and drone inspection is growing. I could be the guy who flies the drone up the tower before anyone climbs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a drone pilot licence in the first six months, even if I pay part of it myself. I'd ask the company to put me on the drone trial. And I'd keep pushing the union to make sure drone work stays with crews, not some outside contractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A little nervous about the cost of the licence, but it feels like a door opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is the licence, and where does it come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About six hundred with the practical. I'd pay it over three months, skip the weekend trips home to see my mum. She'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're pro-union and pro-tech. Does that clash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for me. I want the tech, I just want workers to get the benefit. If drones save money, some of that should come back as pay or training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government and the companies right now, like a fund that pays people while they move. And I'd say it calmly, because panic doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years for the thinking stuff and five for the robots is very fast. The drone idea would buy me a few years, but by 2031 the robots climb the towers and fly themselves. I'd be 32 with a truck loan and almost nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever the robot crews need: setup, repair, remote control. I'd sell the pickup and buy something cheap to kill the loan. And I'd look at moving to wherever the robot maintenance jobs are, even another region.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a bit of adrenaline. Like the first time I climbed a 400-kilovolt tower, scared but focused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really move away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I'm single, renting a room, nothing keeping me. My mum would hate it. But I'd rather move for a job than sit here waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robot maintenance jobs are only for engineers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go back to college, even nights. I'm not great at maths, but I'd use the AI to tutor me. That's what it's good at.

say: We need a **fund** that pays people while they move into new work.
I'd say it **calmly**, because panic doesn't help anyone.
think: Two years for thinking AI and five for robots is **very fast**.
By **2031** robots climb towers, and I'd be 32 with a loan.
do: Learn robot **setup and repair** as early as possible.
Sell the **pickup** and buy something cheap to clear the loan.
Move to wherever the **robot maintenance** jobs are.
feel: **Anxious**, but focused, like his first climb on a **400-kilovolt tower**.

steps.text: Sell the pickup and buy a cheap car to clear the loan

Move to the region with robot maintenance jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent runway if you use it. I'd tell my crew mates that the people who start learning now will be the ones running the robots in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a good spot if I move fast. The planning and dispatch change in 2031, but the climbing stays until about 2034. That's long enough to get the drone licence, a robotics certificate and some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, drone licence and pay off the truck. By year three, a robotics maintenance certificate at the technical college. I'd also try to get the company to pay for it by being on every pilot project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a small worry about money. I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the company won't pay for any of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd pay myself, slowly, and maybe get a weekend job at the electrical wholesaler. It's not ideal, but it's an investment in me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the younger ones the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. I'd tell the apprentices to start learning the robots now and not wait for the company to tell them.

People who start **learning now** will run the robots in 2034.

The climbing stays until about **2034**, long enough to get certificates.

S3.quote: I'd tell the apprentices to start learning the robots now and not wait for the company to tell them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who complains hasn't looked at a calendar. I'd post about it, probably share some courses on the crew chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the best picture for me. Robots arrive around 2039, and I'd be 40, but by then I'd want to be the person programming or fixing them, not climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the five-year plan but slower: drone licence, savings, then a two-year part-time engineering diploma. I'd also look at buying a small share in a local solar co-op, because the grid will need more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited. Ten years is a long time in my world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying into a solar co-op with three weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not now, obviously. Once the truck's paid off, maybe in three or four years. Small amounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that could knock the plan off course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knees, honestly. If I get injured climbing, everything gets harder. Knees are the risk in this job.

I'd share useful **courses** on the crew chat for the others.
think: It's the **best picture** for me, with robots around 2039.
By **40** I'd want to programme or fix robots, not climb.
do: Get the **drone licence** and build savings first.
Start a part-time **engineering diploma** in a few years.
Buy a small share in a **solar co-op** once the truck's paid.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited** about the decade ahead.
S4.quote: If I get injured climbing, everything gets harder. Knees are the risk in this job.
fieldNote: He's **calm** with a decade, driven by his adaptability.

His only real fear is an **injury** stopping his plans.

steps.text: Start a part-time engineering diploma in three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Too fast for someone with a truck loan and no savings. What would help is paid retraining, and companies being made to train their own workers before bringing in robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether we'd still have crews. The best part of this job is the people. Even if a robot climbs, I'd want to be part of a team, not alone with a laptop.

headlineQuote: Even if a robot climbs, I'd want to be part of a team, not alone with a laptop.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old** transmission lineworker who travels the region and lives in a rented room.
He has about **three weeks** saved and a **truck loan** that eats his pay.
He uses AI **every day** and sees drones and robots as a chance to move up.
He backs the **union** but wants workers to share the gains of new tech.
He's **anxious** at AGI by 2028 and **calm** with a decade to prepare.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it's too fast for someone with a loan and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining**, and firms made to train their own workers before bringing in robots.
